column1: What is 'data locality' in HCI, and why does it matter for I/O latency?
column2: Storage I/O from a VM completes within the same physical host where the VM runs, collapsing the I/O path to hypervisor → software storage driver → local NVMe/SSD, dropping latency from hundreds of microseconds (SAN) to tens of microseconds.

column1: How many discrete hardware hops does a traditional three-tier (SAN) I/O path typically cross?
column2: 4–7 hops: hypervisor I/O stack → HBA/NIC → SAN fabric switches → array front-end controller → array cache → back-end disk controller → physical media.

column1: What architecturally distinguishes Hyperconverged Infrastructure (HCI) from Converged Infrastructure (CI)?
column2: CI pre-racks compute+storage from a single vendor but keeps separate management planes (e.g., Vblock running vCenter and EMC Unisphere independently). HCI uses software to dissolve data-plane and administrative boundaries into a single unified management surface.

column1: What are the three invariants a correct HCI implementation must satisfy?
column2: 1) Unified resource pool exposed via a single API/control plane. 2) Software-defined everything (no firmware/hardware touch for policy changes). 3) Convergence of compute, storage, and networking into one coherent system.

column1: What is linearizability of logical addresses in storage virtualization, and why is it stronger than eventual consistency?
column2: If a write to logical block N completes, all subsequent reads from N must return that data or newer writes, regardless of physical remapping — guaranteeing the virtual disk behaves identically to a single perfect physical disk, unlike eventual consistency which allows stale reads.

column1: What is 'bijective mapping consistency' in storage virtualization and what does violating it cause?
column2: At any instant each logical block maps to exactly one physical location, and the physical→logical inverse mapping must be well-defined for GC and rebuilds. Violations cause data corruption or data loss.

column1: State the three Popek-Goldberg virtualization requirements for a VMM.
column2: Efficiency (most guest instructions execute directly on hardware), Equivalence (environment essentially identical to the real machine), and Resource Control (hypervisor maintains complete control over system resources).

column1: Why do VM exits matter for hypervisor performance, and what is their typical cost?
column2: A VM exit is a transition from guest to host mode, costing roughly 500–2000 CPU cycles plus cache pollution. Minimizing VM exit frequency is central to reducing virtualization overhead.

column1: What problem does control-data plane separation (e.g., OpenFlow) solve in network virtualization?
column2: It decouples forwarding decisions (control plane) from packet forwarding execution (data plane), letting a centralized controller compute globally optimal routes and program simple switches via flow tables, instead of each switch making local, uncoordinated decisions.

column1: In HCI management, what is the formula for quorum, and why does it matter for control-plane operations?
column2: Quorum = ⌊N/2⌋ + 1 nodes. Critical operations like VM creation or volume migration require quorum consensus to ensure at most one side of a network partition can make authoritative state changes, preventing split-brain.

column1: State the 'weakest-link' security invariant for an HCI cluster and its formula.
column2: Cluster security S equals the minimum security measure across all nodes: S = min(C_i) for i in 1..n. A single under-patched or misconfigured node becomes the pivot point for lateral movement across the entire cluster.

column1: Why is defense-in-depth 'compensating, not additive' in HCI security, according to Invariant 3?
column2: Layered controls don't multiply independently; if encryption misconfiguration probability is p1 and access control misconfiguration is p2, joint failure is only p1·p2 under independence — but real layers are correlated (e.g., a misconfigured IdP degrades both access control and audit logging), so failure correlations must be analyzed, not just isolated probabilities.
